content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued guidelines on the use of safety-engineered syringes for intramuscular, intradermal, and subcutaneous injections in healthcare settings. These guidelines aim to prevent the reuse of syringes and reduce needle-stick injuries among healthcare workers (HCWs), ultimately improving patient and provider safety while minimizing the transmission of bloodborne infections such as HIV, hepatitis B (HBV), and hepatitis C (HCV). Key Points from the WHO Guidelines: 1. Injection Practices and Risks: Injections are one of the most common medical procedures, with approximately 16 billion administered annually worldwide. About 90% of these are for therapeutic purposes, 5% for immunizations, and the remainder for other uses such as blood transfusions and injectable contraceptives. Unsafe injection practices, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), contribute to the large-scale transmission of bloodborne viruses and bacterial infections. These practices include the reuse of syringes, improper disposal of sharps, and overuse of injections when oral medications are available. 2. Impact of Unsafe Practices: In 2000, WHO estimated that 40% of injections globally were administered with reused equipment, leading to 21 million new HBV cases, 2 million new HCV cases, and 260,000 new HIV cases. Reuse of syringes also increases the risk of bacterial infections and abscesses at injection sites. Needle-stick injuries (NSIs) among HCWs are another significant concern, occurring during or after injections and while handling infected sharps. These injuries expose HCWs to bloodborne infections. 3. Overuse of Injections: In many countries, injections are perceived as more effective and faster-acting than oral medications, leading to their overuse. This includes unnecessary use of antibiotics and injectable vitamins, which may contribute to antimicrobial resistance. 4. Sharps Waste Management: Unsafe disposal of sharps waste, such as incomplete incineration or open dumping, poses risks to HCWs, waste management workers, and the community. In some cases, used syringes are scavenged, repackaged, and resold, further perpetuating unsafe practices. 5. Safety-Engineered Syringes: WHO recommends the use of syringes with safety features, such as reuse prevention (RUP) and sharps injury protection (SIP). These devices are designed to prevent reuse and reduce the risk of NSIs. For example: RUP syringes block reuse after a single aspiration and injection. SIP syringes include mechanisms to protect against sharps injuries, such as features that contain the needle after use. Safety-engineered syringes are well-established in global markets, with performance standards defined by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). 6. Recommendations: WHO conditionally recommends the use of syringes with sharps injury protection (SIP) features for intramuscular, subcutaneous, and intradermal injections to reduce NSIs among HCWs. The use of syringes with reuse prevention (RUP) features is also recommended to prevent the reuse of injection equipment, although the evidence supporting this recommendation is of very low quality. 7. Implementation and Monitoring: The guidelines emphasize the importance of procuring sufficient quantities of safety-engineered syringes and sharps waste management equipment. WHO also plans to launch a global injection safety campaign to reduce the overuse of injections and promote safe practices. The guidelines are intended to support policymakers, healthcare institutions, and manufacturers in adopting and implementing safety-engineered syringes. They also aim to inform HCWs and communities about the importance of safe injection practices. 8. Future Directions: WHO highlights the need for further research to evaluate the effectiveness of safety-engineered syringes and their impact on reducing NSIs and bloodborne infections. The organization also plans to update the guidelines as new evidence becomes available. By addressing unsafe injection practices, promoting the use of safety-engineered syringes, and improving sharps waste management, these guidelines aim to protect patients, HCWs, and communities from preventable harm and infections.
